case_name: Institute of Edible Oil Foods v. Ontario (Ont. H.C.J.)
text:
Re Institute of Edible Oil Foods et al. and The Queen;

Ontario Milk Marketing Board, Intervenor

Indexed as: Institute of Edible Oil Foods v. Ontario

(Ont. H.C.J.)

63 O.R. (2d) 436

[1987] O.J. No. 1189

Ontario

High Court of Justice

McKinlay J.

December 23, 1987.

* An appeal from the following judgment of McKinlay J. to the Ontario Court of Appeal (Blair, Morden and Tarnopolsky JJ.A.) was dismissed with costs on December 15, 1989.  See
1989 CanLII 4232 (ON CA)
, 71 O.R. (2d) 158. A subsequent application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada (Wilson, Sopinka and McLachlin JJ.) was dismissed with costs September 6, 1990.
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Equality rights -- Application to corporations -- Provincial legislation regulating colour of margarine -- Whether discriminatory against margarine producers -- Equality provisions not protecting corporations -- Differentiation also reasonable given objective of protecting stability of dairy industry -- Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, s. 4 --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15
.
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Equality rights -- Provincial legislation regulating colour of margarine -- Whether discriminating against consumers of margarine -- No discrimination -- Objections of consumers of minor importance considering important legislative objective of protecting stability of dairy industry -- Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, s. 4 --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15
.
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Freedom of expression -- Commercial advertising -- Provincial legislation regulating colour of margarine -- Presentation of product a form of advertising -- Advertising included within freedom of expression and regulation violating Charter guarantee -- Regulation reasonable limit under s. 1 -- Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, s. 4 --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1
,
2(b)
.
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Right to life, liberty and security -- Economic rights -- Provincial legislation regulating colour of margarine -- Regulation not infringing right to liberty -- Economic rights not within ambit of Charter guarantee -- Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, s. 4 --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7
.
Section 4 of the Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, which regulates the colouring of margarine, requires that margarine be coloured in a shade either lighter or darker than butter. The applicants sought a declaration that s. 4 is inconsistent with
ss. 2(b)
,
7
and
15
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. Three of the applicants were corporations, two being manufacturers of edible oil products, and the third was a trade association representing the interests of producers and manufacturers of edible oil products. The fourth applicant was an individual consumer.
Held, the application should be dismissed.
Section 4 of the Oleomargarine Act does not violate
s. 15
of the
Charter
. With regard to the first ground of discrimination argued, s. 4 does not discriminate against margarine producers. The claim could be dismissed on a preliminary issue of application because
s. 15
does not provide protection against discrimination to corporate entities, the purpose of the guarantee being to protect the dignity and the worth of human beings. Even if
s. 15
were to apply to protect corporations, s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act would not constitute discrimination against margarine producers. While margarine producers are treated differently from butter producers and suffer a disadvantage because of s. 4, the differential treatment is not unfair or irrational given the legislative objective of protecting the economic stability of the dairy industry. The objections of consumers respecting colour are of minor importance considering the important legislative objective of preserving the economic stability of the dairy industry.
With regard to
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
, the manner in which a product is presented, including its colour, constitutes advertising, which is a form of expression protected by s. 2(b) of the Charter.
Section 4
does infringe the freedom of expression of the corporate applicants. However, the limitation is justified under
s. 1
of the Charter. Its objective of protecting the dairy industry is of substantial economic and social importance and the restriction on freedom of expression is not disproportionate to this important legislative objective.
With regard to
s. 7
of the
Charter
, s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act does not violate the corporate applicants' right to liberty. Economic rights do not fall within the ambit of
s. 7
. As well, s. 4 was enacted for rational social and economic purposes and the evidence does not indicate any violation of the principles of fundamental justice.
APPLICATION for a declaration that s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, violates
ss. 2(b)
,
7
and
15
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and is of no force and effect.

Statutes referred to

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1
,

,

,

Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1)
Dairy Industry Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 45 Oleomargarine Act, 1949, S.O. 1949, c. 66 (later R.S.O. 1960,   c. 268), s. 4 (am. 1962-63, c. 93, s. 1) Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 324, ss. 1(d), 4 (am. 1986,   c. 65, s. 1), 14
Rules and regulations referred to
R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 696 (Oleomargarine Act), ss. 5 (am. O. Reg.   295/84, s. 1), 9(1)(a) (am. idem, s. 3(1))

T. G. Heintzman, Q.C., and H. Underwood, for applicants.
Michael Bader, Q.C., and D. Goldberg, for respondent.
P. Lingard, for intervenor, Ontario Milk Marketing Board.

MCKINLAY J.:-- The applicants request an order declaring that
the provisions of s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act, R.S.O. 1980,
c. 324, as amended (the "Act"), are inconsistent with
ss. 2(b)
,

7
and
15
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, and
accordingly are of no force and effect.

The applicant, the Institute of Edible Oil Foods (the
"Institute"), is an incorporated trade association which
represents the interests of oil seed producers, crushers of oil
seeds, refiners of edible oils, and manufacturers of edible oil
products, including margarines. The corporate applicants,
Thomas J. Lipton Inc. and Nabisco Brands Ltd., are members of
the Institute, refiners of edible oils, and manufacturers of
margarine and other edible oil products. The individual
applicant, Geraldine Saby, is a housewife and mother who
resides with her family in Windsor, Ontario.

In 1927 the Dairy Industry Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 45, was
enacted and, except for a period of time during World War II,
that Act prohibited the manufacture and sale of margarine in
Canada. In 1948 the constitutional validity of the Dairy
Industry Act was tested in Reference re Validity of s. 5(a) of
Dairy Industry Act,
1948 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1949] 1 D.L.R. 433, [1949] S.C.R. 1 and it
was held that in so far as it prohibited the sale, manufacture,
offer for sale, or possession for sale of oleomargarine or
other butter substitutes, the legislation was ultra vires
parliament because it was legislation in respect of property
and civil rights and, consequently, solely within the
provincial legislative authority. As a result of that decision,
the Ontario legislature enacted the Oleomargarine Act, 1949,
S.O. 1949, c. 66, which legalized, for the first time, the
manufacture and sale of margarine in Ontario.

The Act regulates in Ontario the manufacture and sale of
edible oils and margarine. For example, ss. 5 and 9(1)(a) of
the regulations [R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 696] outline precise
requirements for the display of the words "oleomargarine" or
"margarine'' and for the listing of ingredients on packages
containing edible oil or margarine; and s. 14 of the Act
regulates the nature of all margarine advertising. However, the
only section impugned in these proceedings is s. 4, which
regulates the colouring of margarine sold in Ontario. It is s.
4, as amended by 1962-63, c. 93, s. 1, and by 1986, c. 65, s.
1, which is the subject of this application. The effect of s.
4, as amended, is to create one colour range for butter which
approximates its natural colour, and two colour ranges for
margarine, one lighter and one darker than butter. The section
reads:

4. No oleomargarine shall have a tint or shade containing
more than one and six-tenths degrees and less than ten and
one-half degrees of yellow, or of yellow and red
collectively, measured in terms of the Lovibond tintometer
scale or the equivalent of such measurement.

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

1
.  Section 15 -- equality rights

The applicants attack s. 4 of the Act on the basis that it
contravenes the equality rights set out in
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
, which reads:

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under the law
and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit
of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without
discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age, or mental or physical disability.

(a)  Status of corporations

As a preliminary argument, the respondent takes the position
that s. 15(1), referring as it does to every "individual", does
not provide protection against discrimination to corporate
entities.

Montgomery J. in Re Aluminium Co. of Canada Ltd. and The
Queen in right of Ontario (1986),
1986 CanLII 2833 (ON HCJ)
, 55 O.R. (2d) 522 at p. 531,
29 D.L.R. (4th) 583 at p. 593, 25 C.R.R. 50 (Div. Ct.), stated
the following majority view:

... s. 15 is restricted to the protection of individuals and
does not apply to corporate entities. It is a part of the

Charter
that protects the dignity and worth of human beings
against governmental intrusion that would make distinction
between individuals based upon human attributes or
characteristics.

Reid J., in dissent, did not consider it necessary to consider
the effect of the
Charter
and did not comment on the majority
opinion with respect to this issue.

The same conclusion has been reached by a number of courts:
see Milk Board v. Clearview Dairy Farm Inc.,
1987 CanLII 2725 (BC CA)
, [1987] 4 W.W.R.
279, 12 B.C.L.R. (2d) 116; leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused
81
N.R. 240
n; K Mart Canada Ltd./K Mart Canada Ltee v. Millmink
Developments Ltd. (1986),
1986 CanLII 2841 (ON HCJ)
, 56 O.R. (2d) 422, 31 D.L.R. (4th)
135, 24 C.C.L.I. 139 (H.C.J.); Surrey Credit Union v. Mendonca
(1985),
1985 CanLII 264 (BC SC)
, 67 B.C.L.R. 310, 19 C.R.R. 230 (S.C.); Re PPG
Industries Canada Ltd. and A.-G. Can. (1983),
1983 CanLII 287 (BC CA)
, 146 D.L.R. (3d)
261, 3 C.C.C. (3d) 97, 71 C.P.R. (2d) 56 (B.C.C.A.). In Re
Homemade Winecrafts (Canada) Ltd. and A.-G. B.C. (1986),
1986 CanLII 1284 (BC SC)
, 26
D.L.R. (4th) 468 at pp. 471-2 (B.C.S.C.), McKay J. said:

The petitioner is a corporate body and cannot, even with the
most liberal construction, be described as an "individual".
The precise question at issue was determined by McTaggart
L.J.S.C. in Surrey Credit Union v. Mendonca et al. (1985),
1985 CanLII 264 (BC SC)
, 67
B.C.L.R. 310. The learned judge held that the word
"individual" in
s. 15
of the
Charter
does not include a
corporate entity established pursuant to the provisions of
the Credit Union Act. He relied on such cases as R. v.
Colgate Palmolive Ltd. (1971),
1971 CanLII 1232 (ON HCJ)
, 8 C.C.C. (2d) 40, 5 C.P.R.
(2d) 179, which held that the word "individual" in s. 1 of
the Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, does not
encompass a corporate body, and Re PPG Industries Canada Ltd.
and A.-G. Can. (1983),
1983 CanLII 287 (BC CA)
, 146 D.L.R. (3d) 261 at p. 268, 3
C.C.C. (3d) 97, 42 B.C.L.R. 334 (B.C.C.A.) at pp. 338-9, in
which Nemetz C.J.B.C., whilst considering the words "any
person" in s. 11(f) (the right to trial by jury) said
-- "Likewise, under
s. 15
the words 'every individual'
appear to encompass a narrower meaning than 'everyone'." As
well McTaggart L.J.S.C. made mention of the legislative
history of the drafting of the section. I assume he was
referring to the fact that in the Proposed Constitutional
Resolution of October, 1980, the non-discrimination
protections were given to "everyone". The change, in my view,
was to make it abundantly clear that the non-discriminatory
protection afforded by
s. 15
was directed at natural persons.
Human dignity is what is sought to be enhanced and preserved
-- regardless of such personal characteristics as "race,
national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or
mental or physical disability". To hold otherwise would, in
my view, lessen the high ideals enshrined in s. 15 of the
Charter.

The applicants, on the other hand, rely on the decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385, [1985] 1
S.C.R. 295. One of the questions facing the Supreme Court of
Canada in that case was whether or not the provisions of the
Lords Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, prohibiting the sale of
goods on Sundays, infringed the fundamental freedom of
conscience and religion as provided for in
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
. The Attorney-General for Alberta took the position
that the respondent, being a statutory creation, could not be
said to have a conscience or hold a religious belief, and
therefore, it had no right or freedom under
s. 2
(a) which could
be infringed. Responding to that argument, Dickson C.J.C. said,
at pp. 335-7 D.L.R., pp. 313-14 S.C.R.:

Standing and jurisdiction to challenge the validity of a
law pursuant to which one is being prosecuted is the same
regardless of whether that challenge is with respect to
ss.
91
and
92
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
or with respect to
the limits imposed on the Legislatures by the
Constitution
Act, 1982
.

Section 24(1) sets out a remedy for individuals (whether
real persons or artificial ones such as corporations) whose
rights under the
Charter
have been infringed. It is not,
however, the only recourse in the face of unconstitutional
legislation. Where, as here, the challenge is based on the
unconstitutionality of the legislation, recourse to s. 24 is
unnecessary and the particular effect on the challenging
party is irrelevant.

Section 52 sets out the fundamental principle of
constitutional law that the Constitution is supreme. The
undoubted corollary to be drawn from this principle is that
no one can be convicted of an offence under an
unconstitutional law ...

Any accused, whether corporate or individual, may defend a
criminal charge by arguing that the law under which the
charge is brought is constitutionally invalid. Big M is
urging that the law under which it has been charged is
inconsistent with
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and by reason of
s.
52
of the Constitution Act, 1982, it is of no force or
effect.

Whether a corporation can enjoy or exercise freedom of
religion is therefore irrelevant. The respondent is arguing
that the legislation is constitutionally invalid because it
impairs freedom of religion -- if the law impairs freedom of
religion it does not matter whether the company can possess
religious belief. An accused atheist would be equally
entitled to resist a charge under the Act. The only way this
question might be relevant would be if
s. 2
(a) were
interpreted as limited to protecting only those persons who
could prove a genuinely held religious belief. I can see no
basis to so limit the breadth of
s. 2
(a) in this case.

The argument that the respondent, by reason of being a
corporation, is incapable of holding religious belief and
therefore incapable of claiming rights under
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
, confuses the nature of this appeal. A law which
itself infringes religious freedom is, by that reason alone,
inconsistent with s. 2(a) of the Charter and it matters not
whether the accused is a Christian, Jew, Muslim, Hindu,
Buddhist, atheist, agnostic, or whether an individual or a
corporation. It is the nature of the law, not the status of
the accused, that is in issue.

All of the above-cited cases, with the exception of Re PPG
Industries Canada Ltd. and A.-G. Can., supra, were decided
after the release of the decision in R. v. Big M Drug Mart
Ltd., but that decision was not referred to by any of the
courts deciding the other cases.

At first blush, the Big M Drug Mart case would appear to
settle this issue in favour of the applicants. (I can see no
reason to distinguish the two cases on the basis that the Big M
Drug Mart case involves a criminal matter.) However, on more
careful consideration, I do see a substantial difference
between those freedoms protected in
s. 2
of the
Charter
and the
equality rights protected in
s. 15
. The fundamental freedoms
protected by
s. 2
are assured regardless of any qualifying
factor, except a proven justification pursuant to
s. 1
of the
Charter. On the other hand, the equality rights protected by
s.
15
must always be dependent upon the existence of other persons
or groups of persons who are treated differently by the law
than the individual who alleges an infringement of his
s. 15

rights. It follows that there must be some basis upon which he
is treated differently. I agree with Montgomery J.'s decision,
in Re Aluminium Co. of Canada Ltd. and the Queen, supra, where
he concludes that
s. 15
"protects the dignity and worth of
human beings against governmental intrusion ...". It is true
that Montgomery J. would have limited the application of
s. 15

to "distinctions between individuals based upon human
attributes or characteristics"; however, such limitation has
been rejected by the Ontario Court of Appeal in R. v. Ertel,
released June 4, 1987, unreported [since reported
1987 CanLII 183 (ON CA)
, 35 C.C.C.
(3d) 398, 58 C.R. (3d) 252], and in R. v. Century 21 Ramos
Realty Inc. (1987),
1987 CanLII 171 (ON CA)
, 58 O.R. (2d) 737, 37 D.L.R. (4th) 649, 32
C.C.C. (3d) 353. However, I consider it still relevant to the
application of
s. 15
that a corporation of itself cannot
possess human dignity or worth which may be subject to
governmental intrusion. Situations may arise where the nature
of alleged discrimination should and would move the court to
pierce the corporate veil and consider the human
characteristics of members of a corporation. This is not such a
case.

Although Dickson C.J.C., in the Big M Drug Mart case, stated
that "whether a corporation can enjoy or exercise freedom of
religion is ... irrelevant", that statement was based on the
unqualified nature of the freedoms protected in
s. 2
. He
appears to have considered that such a question might be
relevant if
s. 2
(a) were "limited to protecting only those
persons who could prove a genuinely held religious belief".
Such a limitation would be similar to the inherent limitation
in
s. 15
requiring a differentiation in treatment between
individuals or groups.

I therefore consider that the word "individual" as used in
s.
15
of the
Charter
does not include the three corporate
applicants, the Institute of Edible Oil Foods, Thomas J. Lipton
Inc., and Nabisco Brands Limited.

Because of the possibility that I may be in error on the
question of the status of the three corporate applicants under

s. 15
, and because of the existence of the personal plaintiff,
Geraldine Saby, it is necessary for me to consider further the
question of discrimination as alleged by the applicants.

(b)  Legislative purpose

As stated by Dickson C.J.C., in the Big M Drug Mart decision,
in determining the constitutionality of any law, both the
purpose and effect are relevant; however, the initial test is
legislative purpose. If the purpose of the legislation is
invalid because it is intended to interfere with any rights or
freedoms protected by the
Charter
, then it becomes unnecessary
to consider its effect.

It is not disputed that the two stated objectives of the Act,
at the time it was passed in Ontario, were first, the
preservation of the economic stability of the dairy industry in
the province, and second, consumer protection. There can be no
doubt that both are proper legislative objectives which, in
themselves, do not in any way infringe any rights and freedoms
protected by the
Charter
.

The applicants say that these stated purposes are not the
true purposes of the Act. They stress the fact that other
portions of the Act and regulations dealing with packaging and
advertising make it quite clear to the consumer what product he
is purchasing, and thus the consumer protection objective of
the Act is fulfilled by those provisions. Consequently, they
argue, the real purpose of the Act is to discriminate against
margarine producers and consumers, in favour of butter
producers and consumers, by forcing margarine producers to
colour their product so as to dissuade its purchase, and
thereby promote the purchase of butter. The real purpose, they
say, is unacknowledged by the provincial government precisely
because it is aware that s. 4 is per se discriminatory. Thus,
they argue, the discrimination cannot be justified on the
grounds of reasonableness and fairness, and accordingly the
difference in treatment introduced by s. 4 is not pursuant to a
legitimate aim. Were I to accept that position, I would need go
no further, because a statute, the purpose of which is to
infringe a right or freedom protected by the
Charter
, is
obviously unconstitutional pursuant to
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982. However, I am satisfied from the
evidence before me that the two true purposes of the Act are
those which I have already stated. It may be that in furthering
those objectives, the legislature has discriminated against the
applicants, but that in no way affects the legitimacy of the
legislative purposes.

(c)  Legislative effect

It is agreed by both parties that the preservation of the
economic stability of the dairy industry in the province is in
fact advanced by the Act and specifically by the provisions of
s. 4. Indeed, it is the position of the applicants that the
economic advantage to the dairy industry advanced by s. 4 is
the cause of a correlative disadvantage to the producers of
edible oils and margarines, and it is on that undoubted fact
that the position of the corporate applicants under s. 15(1) is
based. Thus, one legitimate legislative objective of the Act
has been advanced by the impugned s. 4; but in the process, say
the corporate applicants, the law has discriminated against
them in a most fundamental way -- by impeding their ability to
compete in the market-place on an equal basis with their only
real competitors -- butter producers.

The respondent takes the position that although protection
from discrimination is not limited to those specific grounds
enumerated in s. 15(1), nevertheless, economic distinctions
created by legislation are not among the grounds for which
relief may be sought. It is true that not every distinction
created by legislation necessarily results in discrimination
within the meaning of s. 15(1): it is the necessary and proper
role of legislators to make distinctions. However, that fact
does not help in the determination of what distinctions made by
governments should be subjected to judicial scrutiny.

The Ontario Court of Appeal, in R. v. Ertel, has established
the steps that should be taken in determining whether
legislation creates discriminatory inequality within the
meaning of s. 15(1).

The first step is to identify the class or classes of persons
who are said to be treated differently. The respondent contends
that s. 4 results in no differential in treatment whatsoever
since the class the legislation is dealing with consists of
producers of edible oils and margarines, and all within that
class are treated equally. No comparison can be drawn to butter
producers, says Crown counsel, because their product is not
subject to the same legislation. I consider such a narrow
definition of class inappropriate in this case. Both butter
producers and margarine producers produce an edible oil product
which is used for the same purposes, and which is presented to
the same over-all market. Section 1(d) of the Act defines
"oleomargarine" to mean "any food substance other than
butter ... that is prepared for the same uses as butter ...". I
am of the opinion that the general class, for the purpose of a
s. 15 analysis, consists of producers of all edible oils
whether in liquid or spread form, and that that general class
includes the two specific classes -- butter producers and
margarine producers.

The second step in the analysis is to determine whether the
two specific classes of edible oil producers are "similarly
situated", since the rule adopted by Morden J.A. in Re McDonald
and The Queen (1985),
1985 CanLII 162 (ON CA)
, 51 O.R. (2d) 745, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 397, 21
C.C.C. (3d) 330, and approved in R. v. Ertel, is that "those
who are similarly situated be treated similarly''. In this
case, such a determination requires the consideration of facts
similar to those in step one. Both butter and margarine
producers produce and sell their product in Ontario; both sell
a product that is used for the same purposes; and both compete
in the same market. I think there can be no doubt that both are
similarily situated.

The third step is to determine whether the corporate
applicants have been dealt with by the legislation "without
discrimination", since it goes without saying that they have in
fact been treated "unequally". Both R. v. Century 21 Ramos
Realty Inc. and R. v. Ertel, supra, instruct us that it is the
"pejorative" approach as described in the Ramos case which
must be applied. Ertel instructs us that in applying that
approach one must first determine whether the legislation
subjects the complaining party to an "inherent disadvantage":
if so, that party is required "to demonstrate the unfairness or
irrationality of the differential treatment which is alleged to
constitute an infringement". There can be no doubt that the
corporate applicants have suffered an inherent disadvantage as
a result of the provisions of s. 4; but, have the applicants
established the unfairness or irrationality of the differential
treatment, keeping in mind the purpose and effect of the
legislation? I think they have not. The legislation is rational
and effective in protecting the economic stability of the dairy
industry, even though in doing so it may be unfair to the
extent that it does not permit complete freedom of competition.
The Court of Appeal of British Columbia, in dealing with a
somewhat similar argument in the case of Milk Board v.
Clearview Dairy Farm Inc., supra, stated at p. 288 W.W.R., p.
125 B.C.L.R.:

Together the arguments challenge regulation of industry. If
accepted, they lead to the conclusion that unregulated free
enterprise is entrenched in our Constitution. That, in the
end, is what the
Charter
arguments amount to and I reject
them.

Such revolutionary consequences could not have been intended.

Dealing with the argument of the personal applicant,
Geraldine Saby, her position is that although consumer
protection may be a true and valid legislative objective, it is
not furthered by the provisions of s. 4. She argues that the
provisions of the Act which provide consumer protection are
those which require licensing of manufacturers and wholesalers,
those which set standards for composition and quality, and
those which regulate the packaging, labelling and advertising
of margarine. Certainly, at the time of purchase, it is not
necessary for any consumer to see the colour of margarine to
distinguish it from butter, because the packaging required by
the Act clearly identifies the package contents. On the other
hand, there is a percentage of margarine sold in Ontario which
may be served to consumers outside of their own homes, and
while it is admitted that this represents a small percentage of
margarine consumed in Ontario, it is possible that consumers
could mistake margarine for butter under such circumstances if
it were not for the required difference in colouring.

I am satisfied that the second legitimate legislative
objective -- consumer protection -- has been advanced by the
impugned s. 4, albeit to a very minor degree; but in the
process, says the personal applicant, the law has discriminated
against her by not allowing her the opportunity (which would be
available but for s. 4) to purchase, in a colour palatable to
her, a product which she may prefer on grounds of
healthfulness, price, or taste.

On the face of it, requiring consumers of margarine to
purchase the product either uncoloured or coloured to such an
unappetizing shade seems both discriminatory and unnecessary.
However, in considering the more important legislative
objective of the Act -- preservation of the economic stability
of the dairy industry in the province, which is undoubtedly
advanced by s. 4 -- the objections of consumers respecting
colour seem to me to be of minor importance. No consumer is
precluded from purchasing or using margarine, and for those who
feel sufficiently strongly about the colour, it is always
possible to buy uncoloured margarine and colour it to a shade
of their choice.

In the result, I find that the provisions of s. 4 of the Act
do not offend
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

2
.  Section 2(b) -- freedom of expression

The applicants argue that s. 4 contravenes the applicants'
freedom of expression as guaranteed by
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter

by preventing margarine producers from colouring their product
in a wholesome and appetizing colour, thereby, communicating to
the public that their product is a desirable one.

I am of the opinion that the manner in which a product is
presented to the public -- its size, shape, colour, texture,
and any other distinguishing feature incorporated into the
product itself -- constitutes a form of advertising which,
although different in type from advertising by words and
pictures, is none the less a form of expression. There is
nothing in
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
to indicate that freedom of
expression should be in any way limited to a particular kind or
class of expression such as political, artistic, or cultural
expression. Indeed, courts have taken a very broad view of
freedom of expression as protected by the Charter. I consider
that the colour in which margarine is presented to the public
constitutes a form of expression which must fall within the
protection of s. 2(b).

Since I find that s. 4 does infringe the right of freedom of
expression of the corporate applicants, I must consider whether
the respondent has satisfied its onus under
s. 1
of the

Charter
. Does s. 4 constitute a reasonable limit to the
applicants' freedom of expression as can be justified in a free
and democratic society? I am satisfied from the evidence
presented by the respondent that protection of the dairy
industry in Ontario is of substantial economic and social
importance. In furthering that objective, the colouring of
margarine as required by s. 4 clearly has a detrimental effect
on both the required methods of production of margarine and on
the portion of the edible oils market likely to be available to
margarine producers. However, such results not unusually follow
the regulation by government of commercial activities. I do not
consider that the restriction on the applicants' freedom of
expression is disproportionate to the very important
legislative objectives involved in this case. Consequently, the
respondent's onus under s. 1 has been satisfied.

3
.  Section 7 -- life, liberty and security of the person

The applicants further challenge the validity of s. 4 of the
Act on the basis that it is constitutionally invalid because it
violates
s. 7
of the
Charter
, which reads:

7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of
the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in
accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

I frankly find it difficult to accept that counsel would
seriously advance a s. 7 argument in a case such as this.
However, the applicants argue that the right to liberty within
the meaning of
s. 7
protects commercial or economic rights,
including the right to market and purchase products in a colour
of one's choice. In my opinion, economic rights do not fall
within the ambit of
s. 7
. In support of that conclusion see Re
Malartic Hygrade Gold Mines (Canada) Ltd. and Ontario
Securities Com'n (1986),
1986 CanLII 2653 (ON HCJ)
, 54 O.R. (2d) 544, 27 D.L.R. (4th) 112,
24 C.R.R. 1 (Div. Ct.); Re Aluminium Co. of Canada, Ltd. and
The Queen, supra; Re Gershman Produce Co. Ltd. and Motor
Transport Board (1985),
1985 CanLII 127 (MB CA)
, 22 D.L.R. (4th) 520, [1986] 1 W.W.R.
303, 36 Man. R. (2d) 81 (C.A.); R. v. Video Flicks Ltd. (1984),

1984 CanLII 44 (ON CA)
, 48 O.R. 395, 14 D.L.R. (4th) 10, 15 C.C.C. (3d) 353 (C.A.);
affirmed as to s. 7,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, 35 D.L.R. (4th) 1, 30 C.C.C. (3d) 385,
[1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, sub nom. Edwards Books & Art Ltd. v.
The Queen. In any event, s. 4 was enacted by the provincial
legislature for rational social and economic purposes, and none
of the evidence filed before me indicates that any principles
of fundamental justice have been violated in this case.

The application is dismissed with costs.

Application dismissed.
